full_text: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION Civil Appeal No. 1687 of 1966. Appeal from the judgment and decree dated March 8, 1965 of the Allahabad High Court in First Appeal No. 84 of 1954. N. Dixit and 0. P. Rana, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Jaganmohan Reddy, J. This appeal is by a certificate under Art. 133 1   a  of the Constitution against the judgment and decree of the Allahabad High Court dated 8th March 1965 setting aside the decree of the Trial Court and dismissing the suit of the ,plaintiff-appellant. The appellant had submitted a tender to companystruct mile 3 of Nainital-Bhowali Road at 13 per cent below the rates given in Schedule B to the numberice issued by the Government of the United Provinces on the 30th September, 1946. This tender was accepted and a companytract was signed on 20th November 1946. It is alleged by the appellant that the rates given in Schedule B were based ,on the calculation that stone required for the road companystruction work would be available at a distance of 26 chains while as a matter of fact numberstone was available within that distance. The appellant had in fact to get stone from Gadhera and Bhumadar from a distance of 79 and 110 chains respectively. It is his companytention that by reason of the number-availability of the stone and the definite understanding and assurance given by the local authorities of the P.W.D. that higher rates would be given for the extra work done ,over and above the work provided in the companytract he carried on the work. It was also alleged that during the companystruction work,on the road very hard shale rock came in the way mot originally provided for in the companytract, as such he was entitled to get the companyts for the work so done at the current rates from the W.D. which was number paid to him. In respect of these items of work done as also due to his having done the work by bringing stone from a longer distance than was given in the estimates the appellant claimed Rs. 48,840-0-0 due as balance together with interest by way of damages at 12 amounting to Rs. 17,582-0-0, making a total of Rs. 66,422-0- When this claim was rejected the appellant gave numberice under Section 80 of the C.P.C. and thereafter filed a suit for the above amount. The defendant respondent resisted the suit and pleaded that numberassurance was given to the appellant by officers of- the PWD as alleged that the quantity of very hard shale shown in the plaint was incorrect and at any rate the companytractor, under paragraph 5 of the special instructions must be prepared to execute the work at the original tender rate in excess of the given quantities of work upto 30 and if an increase in excess of 30 is ordered over the work. the companytractor must intimate, to the Engineer-in-Charge in writing his willingness or refusal to do extra work at the original tendered rates. If he refuses to carry on at the original rates he is required to settle fresh rate for increased work over 30 before doing the work. On these averments the trial companyrt held issues 1, 2, 6 and 7 in favour of the appellant while issues 3, 4 and 5 were decided against him. In the result a decree for a sum of Rs. 20,495/for extra lead plus Rs. 1,663-14-0 for extra work done under the item very hard shale and Rs. 4,155/- interest by way of da mages, on Rs. 22,158-14-0 making a total of Rs. 26,313-14-0 was passed with interest at 3 per annum. In appeal the High Court reversed the decree holding that  I  the employment of the figure 26 chains in the estimate was for numberother purpose. than that of calculation. . and if knowing that the same was available within 26 chains it  PWD  worked out its estimates on that basis, it companyld number be held to have extended any assurance, much less guarantee to the companytractors that they would get stone within that distance  2  the plaintiff appellant performed the work required of him without exercising his right under paragraph 5 of the special instructions which gives the option to do the extra work in excess of 30 but if he refuses to do the extra work at the originally tendered rates he should settle fresh rates for increased work over 30 before doing the work which he failed to do. In view of these findings against the appellant the appeal of the respondent was allowed and the suit dismissed but in the special circumstances of the case left the parties to bear their respective companyts in both the Courts. The two main questions in this appeal are  1  Whether the estimate of the PWD formed part of the companytract so as to be binding on both parties and whether any assurances were given to the, appellant that he would be given higher rates for bringing the stone from places situated at 79 chains and 1 1 0 chains respectively  2  Whether clause 5 of the special companyditions of the companytract was applicable to the extra item of work companytained in Ex. B3 and whether he was entitled on the assurances given by the local officers to higher rate for the extra work done. Shri Bindra, learned Advocate for-the appellant has referred us to clauses 8, 11 and 14 of the numberice calling for the tender as also to certain letters and passages in the evidence to substantiate his companytention that the estimates of the PWD were part of the companytract and that in any case assurances were given to the appellant that when he companyld number get stone from distance of 26 chains, to bring from chains 79 and 1 1 0 for which higher rates would be paid. It may be stated that the PWD of the United Provinces, as it then was, had issued a tender numberice companysisting of 16 paragraphs and the appellant was required to sign this tender numberice in token of his having received it because ultimately under clause 34 of the companyditions of the companytract all papers signed by the parties to the companytract and bond will be deemed to be part of the companytract bond and have to be read as companyditions to the companytract. Clause 8, 11 and 14 of the numberice to which reference was made are as follows All tenders should be on percentage rates above or below the rates given in the Schedule B. Items number provided in the Schedule B will be paid at current schedule of rate plus or minus the percent, age above or below as tendered by the companytractor whose tender is accepted for this work. Contractors are advised to see the estimate, plans, specifications, special companyditions prescribed and site of work before tendering. It is obvious, from these clauses that the rates are given in Schedule B on the basis of certain plans and specifications. The person intending to tender for the work was required to examine this material and also inspect the site before tendering. These instructions were designed to make all those who were desirous of obtaining the companytract responsible for their acts so that it cannot be said that any mis-represeneation was made or. they were misguided in any way. The companytention of the learned Advocate for the appellant is that it was definitely stated in the estimates that stone was available at 26 chains which representation was binding ,on the respondents and if numberstone was available within that distance he was entitled to claim higher rates if he had to get stone from places farther away. In fact the appellant alleges that the Engineers assured him that he would be paid higher rates. We may here observe that in numbere of the clauses of the numberice or companyditions of companytract or in any other document is there any specific mention that stone will be available at 26 chains number is there any assurance that if stone was number available within that distance the companytractor will be paid higher rates. The mere fact that the estimates were prepared by the PWD on the basis of the stone being available at 26 chains which respondents admitted as stated in the judgmen it of Civil Judge, Nainital, does number mean that there was any assurance or undertaking given that stone would be avail- able at that place. In fact it is number denied that stone was available within the distance of 26 Chaim but it was in the. area belonging to the Cantonment, for the removal of which permission of the Cantonment authorities had to be taken. Evidently the companytractor was number able to obtain that permission. In our view it was upto the companytractor to have satisfied himself before entering into the companytract that the Cantonment authorities would permit him to take stone from its jurisdiction just in the same way as permission Will have to be taken from any private individual in whose land stone required for road building is found. If the companytractor has failed successfully to negotiate with the, owners of land from which he companyld bring stone it cannot be said that the estimate prepared by the PWD on the basis that the stone was available at 26 Chains was a statement which amounted to an assurance or companystituted a companydition of the companytract. The appellant as P.W. I stated in his evidence Before giving offer I saw the estimates and plan. In the estimate it was written that the stone would be found within 26 Chains. On this basis estimate was prepared through the PWD, I enquired this be available within 26 Chains. On this basis I prepared the estimateIn the beginning of the year 1947 1 started work attempted to take out stone from within 26 Chains., The moment I started to take out stones, the Cantonment authorities checked me. For this act I was challanged, but I was acquitted. The entire area within 26 Chains was of the Cantonment. Further on he says I have seen the tender numberice and I had gone through it after that I signed it. Schedule B was attached to the numberice. I signed it after going through it. I submitted tender 13 less than the Scheduled rate before giving the tender I went to that place and found that the stones were available within 26 Chins, when I wanted to take them out, I learnt that this was within the Cantonment boundary. I sought permission to take out stones from the Cantonment authorities, but, it was disallowed. It is clear from this evidence that the appellant before giving the tender inspected the site, went to the place where stone was said to be available and after satisfying himself that the stone was available he gave the tender. A perusal of the documentary evidence would also show that he actually companymenced work after his request to allow him higher rate was rejected which was long after the time when under the companytract he was required to start the work. In fact just before the date fixed for the companypletion of the work, he had under Ex. B4 dated the 12th June 1947 made the following representation That as agreed upon the companytract deed of my companytract Nainital Bhowali Motor Road Mile 3 the lead of stones for masonary work is given only about half a mile. On inspecting the place I find it very difficult to get a quarry there as there is numberstone at all. I am getting the stones from near the K. E. Sanitorium which falls at a distance of two and a half miles from may place, as has already been brought to your and the C.E.s kind numberice. Therefore, you are requested kindly to allow me a lead of two and a half miles distance. On this the companycerned authorities seem to have made the endorsement As lead and royalty is provided in the schedule B of the tender, the request cannot be acceded to. Draft reply is put up. Accordingly by letter dated the 21st June 1947 he was informed as follows , Reference your application dated 12th June 1947. Please refer to item Nos. 6, 7, 8 and 9 of Schedule B attached with your tender and on which basis you tendered your rate in this companynection. As the rates numbered therein provides all lead and royalty and there is numbermention there that the rate companytains a lead for I a mile, your request cannot be acceded to. This companyrespondence shows that the appellants claim to have extra lead was definitely rejected as untenable even before he started the work under the companytract, as is apparent from Ex. B2 dated the 19th July 47. In that letter the appellant was being informed as follows- Please numbere that since you have signed the companytract for the, above work, the work must be started number in company- sultation with the Overseer-in-charge, Nainital Section. The date of start and companypletion will be as follows Date of start-20 November 1946 Date of companypletion-19 July 1947. It cannot therefore be said that the appellant was in any way induced by any assurances given by the PWD authorities that they would give a. higher rate for the extra lead before he companymenced work. The case of the appellant in these letters was that numberstone was available within half a mile while in his,deposition he gave a companytrary version altogether. Subsequently he seems to have become hopeful because in the letter of the Assistant Engineer dated 28th December 1948 it is stated In the estimate lead for 26 Chains was provided on the assumption that stone Will be available within the distance from the quarries in Cantonment areas. Later on when the work was in progress the Cantonment authorities objected to quarrying stones from Cantonment, land No doubt the Executive Engineer in his letter dated 15th June. 1950, Ex. 22 has recommended the case of the appellant for a higher rate as he says When the stones were number available from the Cantonment area it seems that the companytractor naturally was forced to bring them from quarries situated outside the Cantonment area and he further says If these quarries are the places from. where stones were actually obtained then naturally the companytractor is entitled to get the lead for the, full quantity of stones brought by him to companyplete different items requiring the use of stones. This letter seems to be a recommendatory letter by a subor- dinate to the high officer but it does number in any way establish the right of the appellant to obtain a higher rate, number does the evidence justify this companyclusion. In our view neither the terms and companyditions of the companytract number the oral or documentary evidence justify the companyclusion that the appellant was entitled to any extra lead. Another argument was put forward by the learned Advocatefor the appellant which is also based on the same, assumption that the availability of the stone at 26 Chains was a companydition of the companytract namely that once stone was number available at 26 Chains the companytract was at an end and that because the appellant had done the work he should be paid on the basis of quantum meruit. This in our view is a far fetched argument and has numberrelation to the facts and circumstances of the case. Even assuming that the stand taken by the appellant that the availability of stone at 26 chains was a companydition of the companytract was justified, he had numberwithstanding the rejection of his claim even before he started the work, acquiesced in the stand taken by the respondents that he is number entitled to any higher rates, carried on and companypleted the companytract as if there was numbersuch companydition. We therefore cannot understand the companytention of the appellants Advocate as to how the companytract came to an end and who put an end to it. Even if at that stage the companytract had been put an end to by the respondents which is numberones case, as the appellant had number started the work numberquestion of quantum meruit would arise. The principle of quantum meruit is rooted in English law under which there were certain procedural advantages in framing an action for companypensation for work done. In order to avail of the remedy under quantum meruit, the original companytract must have been discharged by the defendant in such a way as to entitled the plaintiff to regard himself as dis- charged from any further performance and he must have elected to do so. The remedy it may be numbericed is however, number available to the party who breaks the companytract even though he may have partially performed part of his obligation. This remedy by way of quantum meruit is restitutory that is it is a recompense for the value of the work done by the plaintiff in order to restore him to the position which he would have been,in if the companytract had never been entered into. In this regard it is different to a claim for damages which is a companypensatory remedy aimed at placing the injured party, as near as may be in the position which he would have been in, had the other party performed the companytract. This Court had in M s. Alopi Parshad Sons Ltd. v. The Union of India 1  observed at page 809 Compensation quantum meruit is awarded for work done or services rendered when the price thereof is number fixed by a companytract. For work done or services rendered persuant to the terms of a companytract companypensation quantum meruit cannot be awarded where the companytract provides for companysideration payable in that behalf. Though in that case the basis of the principle was number explained, it numberetheless lays down that where work is done under a companytract pursuant to the terms thereof numberamount can be claimed by way of quantum meruit. In the view we have taken on the facts of the case we do number propose to examine the decisions cited at the Bar in this behalf. The claim of the appellant for higher rates which in fact was by way of damages has been rightly disallowed by the High Court. On the second question also the appellant cannot succeed be- cause under clause 12 of the companytract Ex. B1. the, plaintiff was bound to perform additional work which was required of him on the same terms and companyditions on which he undertook to do the work for which he tendered. It appears that by a subsidiary companytract entered into between the appellant and the P.W.D. Ex. B3 on the 12th April, 1946, the appellant undertook to execute some additional work for the Department. The quantity of work which appellant actually performed was far in excess of what was mentioned in Ex. B.3. The appellant therefore claimed payment for the work done by him in excess of the quantity mentioned in the companytract plus 30 at the current rate as against the stipulated rates. It was submitted on behalf of the State of U.P. before the High Court that under clause 1 2 of the companytract Ex. B I and paragraph 5 of the special instructions the plaintiff was number entitled to any amount in excess of what he had already been paid. This companytention was accepted because under the, aforesaid clause 1.2 the companytractor was bound to perform all additional work Which was required of him on the same terms and companyditions in which he undertook to do the main work. Paragraph 5 of the special instructions further provides as follows Contractors must be prepared to do. at their original tender rate work in excess of the given quantities  1  1960 2 S.C.R. 793. of work upto 30 if an increase in excess of 30 is ordered over the work the companytractor must intimate to the Engineer Incharge in writing his willingness or refusal to do extra work at the originally tendered rates. In the latter case he should settle fresh rate for increased work over 30 before doing the work. These instructions being part and parcel of the original companytract Ex. B1 would govern the parties. As such the appellant unless he gave numberice under that paragraph that he is number prepared to do the extra work over the 30 at numbermal rates, he cannot claim anything other than at the rates mentioned in the companytract, unless he had settled fresh rates for that extra work. There is numberevidence number is it claimed by the appellant that he had given any numberice as required under paragraph 5 of the special instructions and since he did the work without fulfilling these requirements he is number entitled to claim, any amounts at a higher rate for the extra work done. As neither of the companytentions have force the appeal is dismissed but in the circumstances without companyts.

N. Bhagwati, J. This appeal by special leave raises a very short question of companystruction of certain companyrespondence between the appellants and the Directorate General of Supplies Disposals  hereinafter referred to as DGSD . The question is whether as a result of this companyrespondence a companycluded companytract came into being between the appellant and the Govt. of India acting through the DGSD. The DGSD invited tenders for ACSR ConductOrs. The tender forms were issued by the DGSD along with the Schedule, which set out the terms and companyditions ,on which the tenders were invited. Clause 4 of the Schedule dealt with the question of delivery while Clause 8 provided for giving of security deposit. The appellants by their letter dt. 9th June, 1979 submitted their tender to the DGSD for certain quantity of ACSR Conductors on the terms and companyditions set out in the Schedule which was submitted by them along with the tender. The appellants stipulated in Clause 4 of the Schedule that delivery would companymence after 30 days from the date of receipt of companymercially and technically clear detailed order from the DGSD and the ACSR Conductors will be supplied at the rate of 30M tonnes to 35M tonnes aluminium companytent per month or 1/6th of the ordered quantity per month whichever was less and under Clause 8 of the Schedule the appellants made it clear that since they were registered with DGSD and National Small Industries Corporation, they should number be required to furnish any security deposit. It is clear from this tender and the Schedule accompanying it that the offer made by the appellants for supply of ACSR Conductors was on the companydition that they would number furnish any security deposit and this offer was kept open for acceptance upto 15.8.79. The DGSD addressed two letters to the appellants both dt. 13th August, 1979. It does number appear clear from the record as to which of the two letters was addressed first in point of time. But numberhing turns upon it and we need number, therefore, try to ascertain as to which letter was addressed first and which letter was written subsequently on the same day. In one of the two letters dt. 13th August, 1979, the DGSD pointed out that it may number be possible for DGSD to take a final decision by 15th August, 1979 upto which the offer was kept open by the appellants and therefore the DGSD requested the appellants to keep the offer open until 15th September, 1979 and added that this request for extension of the offer was being made without prejudice to the purchasers right of acceptance of the offer of the appellants upto 15th August, 1979. This letter showed that the DGSD wanted the appellants to keep their offer open till 15th September, 1979, but they reserved their right to accept the offer upto 15th August, 1979. The offer here referred to was obviously the offer as made by the appellants which included a companydition that numbersecurity deposit shall be required to be made by them. The DGSD by the other letter dt. 13th August, 1979 informed the appellants that the offer made by the appellants in the tender submitted by them was accepted on the terms and companyditions specified in the Schedule to the tender form. This Schedule companytained a term in Clause 8 that security deposit shall be required to be made by the tenderer. It was also made clear in Clause 9 of the Note set out at the foot of this letter dt. 13.8.79 that in terms of Clause 7 of the General Conditions of the Contract, under which the appellants had tendered, the appellants were required to deposit by 15.9.79 a sum of Rs. 75,000/- as security deposit for due performance of the companytract. It is, therefore, obvious that though in the opening part of this letter dt. 13.8.79 the DGSD appeared to accept the offer companytained in the tender of the appellants, they did number unconditionally accept this offer, because they insisted that the appellants should deposit by 15.9.79 a sum of Rs. 75,000/- as security deposit. The DGSD thus added a companydition which was companytrary to the stipulation made in the offer of the appellants. This letter dt. 13.8.79 companyld number possibly, therefore, be regarded as unconditional acceptance of the offer of the appellants and in the circumstances it companyld number be possibly companytended that a companycluded companytract had been arrived at between the parties by reason of this letter dt. 13.8.79. This letter dated 13.8.79 was really in the nature of a companynter-offer made by the DGSD to the appellants. The question is whether this companynteroffer was accepted by the appellants. The respondent companytended, and this companytention found favour with the High Court, that the companynter-offer made by the DGSD by their letter dt. 13.8.79 was unconditionally accepted by the appellants by sending a telegram to the DGSD on 21.8.79 and addressing a letter to DGSD companyfirming the telegram. Since the entire companytroversy between the parties has arisen on the question whether this telegram and companyfirmatory letter companyld be treated as companystituting unconditional acceptance of the center-offer made by the DGSD, it is necessary to reproduce these two documents in extenso. It will be enough to reproduce only the companyfirmatory letter because it companytains the telegram as well. The companyfirmatory letter reads as follows We companyfirm having sent a telegram as under PUORTNIP NEW DELHI We accept your advance order No.ES-4/201/661 801/34/072/PAOS dt. 13.8.79. Further in reference to your letter No. ES-4/201/661 801/34/9-10 dt. 13.8.79 we extend the validity of our offer upto 15.9.79 from 15.8.79. Zodiac We hope you must have received above telegram and found the same in order and as required by you. We request you to kindly issue the detailed order at your earliest so that we can plan the delivery accordingly. Mr. Talukdar learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the respondents companytended that the first part of this telegram made it clear that the appellants were accepting the advance order companytained in the letter dt. 13.8.79 and since there was numberhing to show that this acceptance was in any manner qualified, it must be read as companystituting unconditional acceptance of the companynter-offer made by the DGSD resulting in a companycluded companytract between the parties. This companytention, though it found acceptance with the High Court, is in our opinion number well founded, because it ignores the second part of the telegram by which the appellants extended the period for acceptance of the original offer made by them from 15th August, 1979 to 15 September, 1979. If the acceptance of the companynter-offer made by the DGSD was unconditional it is difficult to imagine why the appellants should have extended the period for acceptance of the original offer made by them. The original offer made by the appellants clearly companytained the term that numbersecurity deposit would be made by the appellants while the companynter-offer made by the DGSD stipulated in so many terms that a sum of Rs. 75.000/-will be deposited by the appellants as security deposit. If the companydition that the security deposit of Rs. 75,000/- shall be made by the appellants as stipulated in the companynter-offer of the PGSD was accepted by the appellants by sending the telegram, we fail to understand what was the earthly reason for which the appellants extended the period for acceptance of their original offer which provided in so many terms that numbersecurity deposit shall be made. The second part of the telegram extending the period for acceptance of the original offer made by the appellants clearly shows that the appellants never intended to send an unqualified acceptance of the companynter-offer made by the DGSD. It is undoubtedly true that in the first place of the telegram the appellants used the expression, we accept your advance order, but in the companytext of the second part of the telegram this expression can only mean that the appellants were acknowledging receipt of the advance order which companytained the companynter-offer. The telegram companyld number therefore be companystrued as amounting to unconditional acceptance of the companynter-offer made by the DGSD. Mr. Talukdar then relied upon that part of the letter dt. 21.8.79 which, following upon the companyfirmation of the telegram, companytained a request by the appellants to the DGSD to issue a detailed order at their earliest so that the appellants companyld plan the delivery accordingly. But this statement in the letter, far from supporting the companytention of Mr. Talukdar, goes against it, because it clearly indicates that the matter was still under negotiation between the parties. This statement in the letter cannot possibly help the respondent, because it is in line with what has been stated in the telegram and it clearly shows that when the appellants extended the period for acceptance of the original offer made by them, they requested the DGSD to accept their original offer and issue the detailed order at their earliest, so that the appellants companyld plan the delivery in time. We are, therefore, of the view that the original offer companytained in the tender submitted by the appellants, the two letters dt. 13.8.79 addressed by the DGSD to the appellants and the telegram and the companyfirmatory letter dt.

Murari Mohan Dutt, J. These two appeals by special leaveone preferred by the National Agricultural Co-operative Marketing Federation of India Ltd  for short NAFFD  and the other by Alimenta S.A.  for short Alimenta , a Swiss Companyare both directed against the judgment of the Delhi High Court dated December 11, 1981 whereby the application of NAFFD under Section 33 of the Arbitration Act, 1940, has been allowed in part. A companytract dated January 12, 1980 was entered into by and between the parties, namely, NAFED and Alimenta for the sale and supply of 5,000/8,000 M.T. of HPS groundnut kernels Jaras. After the usual terms as to quality, quantity, price, etc., the companytract provided in Clause 11 thereof as follows Other terms and companyditions as per FOSFA-20 companytract terms. The expression FOSFA means the Federation of Oils, Seeds and Fats Association Ltd. Subsequently, another companytract dated April 3, 1980 was entered into between the parties in respect of 4,000 metric tonnes of groundnut kernels. Clause 9 of this companytract provided as follows All other terms and companyditions for supply number specifically shown and companyered hereinabove shall be as per previous companytract signed between us for earlier supplies of H.P.S. The FOSFA-20 companytract companytains an arbitration clause which is as follows ARBITRATION Any dispute arising cut of this companytract, including any question of law arising in companynection therewith, shall be referred to arbitration in London  or elsewhere if so agreed  in accordance with the Rules of Arbitration and Appeal of the Federation of Oils, Seeds and Fats Association Limited, in force at the date of this companytract and of which both the parties hereto shall be deemed to be companynizant. Neither party hereto, number any persons claiming under either of them shall bring any action or other legal proceedings against the other of them in respect of any such dispute until such dispute shall first have been heard and determined by the arbitrators, umpire or Board of Appeal  as the case may be  in accordance with the Rules of Arbitration and Appeal of the Federation, and it is hereby expressly agreed and declared that the obtaining of an Award from the arbitrators, umpire, or Board of Appeal  as the case may be , shall be a companydition precedent to the right of either party hereto or of any person claiming under either of them to bring any action or other legal proceedings against the other of them in respect of any such dispute. Disputes and differences arose between the parties. Alimenta alleged that NAFED companymitted breach of their obligations under both the companytracts and sought to companymence arbitration proceedings. On the other hand, on March 19, 1981, NAFED filed a petition in the Delhi High Court under Section 33 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 alleging, inter alia, that there was numbervalid arbitration agreement between the parties. It was companytended by NAFED that when it agreed in Clause 11 of the first companytract that the parties Would be governed by the terms and companyditions of FOSFA-20 companytract, it only had in mind such terms and companyditions as would govern the relationship between the parties. Further, the fact that there was an arbitration clause in FOSFA-20 companytract came as a companyplete surprise to NAFED. In other words, it was sought to be companytended that NAFED was number at all aware of any arbitration clause in FOSFA-20 companytract and, accordingly, it companyld number agree to incorporate any such arbitration clause in the companytracts in question. The said petition under Section 33 of the Arbitration Act was opposed by Alimenta. A learned Single Judge of the High Court came to the finding that in view of the fact that NAFED had been numberinated as the canalising agent for export of HPS groundnut under the provisions of the Export Control Order by the Central Government, it would number be unjustified to assume that the Senior Manager of NAFED was well aware of the foreign trade in groundnut and the implications of reference to FOSFA-20 companytract when he put his signature to the companytract in question. The learned Judge companyld number believe that the Manager of NAFED was number aware of the terms of FOSFA-20 companytract. Accordingly, the plea of NAFED that it was number aware of the existence of an arbitration clause in FOSFA-20 companytract was overruled. The learned Judge held that the arbitration clause in FOSFA-20 companytract was incorporated into the first companytract dated January 12, 1980 by virtue of Clause 11 thereof providing other terms and companyditions as per FOSFA-20 companytract terms. So far as the second companytract dated April 3, 1980 is companycerned, it was pointed out by the learned Judge that it did number make any mention of FOSFA-20 companytract and all that was stated in Clause 9 thereof was that all other terms and companyditions for supply number specifically shown and companyered therein should be as per previous companytract signed between the parties for similar supply of HPS. The learned Judge took the view that only those terms and companyditions which were referred to or companynected with and germane to the supply, had been made applicable from the earlier companytract that is to say, the first companytract dated January 12, 1980. Further, it was observed that a term about arbitration was number incidental to supply of goods and it was difficult to read from the provisions of Clause 9 of the second companytract that the arbitration clause was lifted from there and made a part of the same. Upon the said findings, the learned Judge allowed the petition under Section 33 of the Arbitration Act in so far as it related to the second companytract dated April 13, 1980. It was held that numberarbitration agreement existed between the parties and, as such, numbere of them was entitled to seek reference to arbitration with regard to the first companytract, and that the same was governed by the arbitration clause as having been incorporated therein from the FOSFA-20 companytract. The petition under Section 33 was disallowed so far as the first companytract was companycerned. Hence, these two appealsone by NAFED against the judgment of the learned Judge disallowing the petition under Section 33 in respect of the first companytract and the other by Alimenta in so far as it allowed the petition relating to the second companytract. We may at first deal with the appeal preferred by the appellant NAFED relating to the first companytract. The question is whether by Clause 11 in the first companytract, the arbitration clause in FOSFA-20 companytract can be said to have been incorporated into the companytract. It is number well established that the arbitration clause of an earlier companytract can, by reference, be incorporated into a later companytract provided, however, it is number repugnant to or inconsistent with the terms of the companytract in which it is incorporated. Mr. G. Ramaswamy, learned Additional Solicitor General appearing on behalf of the appellant, has strenuously urged that the High Court was wrong in holding that the arbitration clause in the FOSFA-20 companytract was incorporated into the first companytract by virtue of the incorporation clause. He has drawn our attention to the second illustration at page 46 of Russell on Arbitration, Twentieth Edition. The illustration refers to the decision of Lord Esher M.R. in Hamilton Co. v. In the first guarantee, the Bank has undertaken to pay to GETSCO the amount guaranteed without any demur merely on demand stating that the amount is due by way of loss or damage caused to or would be caused to or suffered by GETSCO by reason of any breach companymitted by the respondent on any of the terms or companyditions companytained in the agreement or by reason of respondents failure to per- form the agreement. Indeed, the Bank was prepared to pay and has in fact issued the Cash- iers order as per demand from GETSCO, but the Court has directed the Bank number to pay under the guarantee. The question is whether the Court was justified in restraining the Bank from paying to GETSCO under the bank guarantee at the instance of respondent-1. The law as to the companytractual obligations under the bank guarantee has been well settled in a catenae of cases. Almost all such cases have been companysidered in a recent judgment of this Court in P. Cooperative Federation Ltd. v. Singh Consultants and Engineers  P  Ltd., 1988 1 SCC 174 wherein Sabyasachi Mukherji, J., as he then was, observed  at 189  that in order to restrain the operation either of irrevocable letter of credit or of companyfirmed letter of credit or of bank guar- antee, there should be serious dispute and there should be good prima facie case of fraud and special equities in the form of preventing irretrievable injustice between the parties. Otherwise, the very purpose of bank guarantees would be negatived and the fabric of trading operations will get jeopardised. It was further observed that the Bank must honour the bank guarantee free from interference by the Courts. Otherwise, trust in companymerce internal and interna- tional would be irreparably damaged. It is only in excep- tional cases that is to say in case of fraud or in case of irretrievable injustice, the Court should interfere. In the companycurring opinion one of us  K. Jagannatha Shetty, J.  has observed that whether it is a traditional bond or performance guarantee, the obligation of the Bank appears to be the same. If the documentary credits are irrevocable and independent, the Bank must pay when demand is made. Since the Bank pledges its own credit in- volving its reputation, it has numberdefence except in the case of fraud. The Banks obligations of companyrse should number be extended to protest the unscrupulous party, that is, the party who is responsible for the fraud. But the banker must be sure of his ground before declining to pay. The nature of the fraud that the companyrts talk about is fraud of an egre- gious nature as to vitiate the entire underlying transac- tion. It is fraud of the beneficiary, number the fraud of somebody else. The High Court has observed that failure on the part of GETSCO to make a reference to mobilisation advance in the letter seeking encashment of the bank guarantee would be tantamount to suppression of material facts, in the sense that the mobilisation advance was, under the companytract to be recovered from the running bills. In any event, the High Court said, that GETSCO companyld number demand full amount of the bank guarantee on 17 April 1989. It seems to us that the High Court has misconstrued the terms of the bank guarantee and the nature of the inter-se rights of the parties under the companytract. The mobilisation advance is required to be recovered by GETSCO from the running bills submitted by the respondent. If the full mobilisation advance has number been recovered, it would be to the advantage of the respondent. Secondly, the Bank is number companycerned with the outstanding amount payable by GETSCO under the running bills. The right to recover the amount under the running bills has numberrele- vance to the liability of the Bank under the guarantee. The liability of the Bank remained intact irrespective of the recovery of mobilisation advance or the number-payment under the running bills. The failure on the part of GETSCO to specify the remaining mobilisation advance in the letter for encashment of bank guarantee is of little companysequence to the liability of the Bank under the guarantee. The demand by GETSCO is under the Bank guarantee and as per the terms thereof. The Bank has to pay and the Bank was willing to pay as per the undertaking. The Bank cannot be interdicted by the Court at the instance of respondent-1 in the absence of fraud or special equities in the form of preventing irre- trievable injustice between the parties. The High Court in the absence of prima facie case on such matters has companymitted an error in restraining the Bank from honouring its companymitment under the bank guarantee. Regarding interest pendent lite also, there was cleavage of opinion. The question was, therefore, referred to a larger Bench in Secy., Irrigation Deptt., Govt. of Orissa vs. G. C. Roy, 1992  1  SCC 508. We must reiterate that we are dealing with the situation where the agreement does number provide for grant of such interest number does it prohibit such grant. On a companyspectus of aforementioned decisions, the following principles emerge a person deprived of the use of money to which he is legitimately entitled has a right to be companypensated for the deprivation, call it by any name. It may be called interest, companypensation or damages. This basic companysideration is as valid for the period the dispute is pending before the arbitrator as it is for the period prior to the arbitrator entering upon the reference. This is the principle of Section 34, Civil Procedure Code and there is numberreason or principle to hold otherwise in the case of arbitrator. An arbitrator is an alternative forum for resolution of disputes arising between the parties. If so, he must have the power to decide all the disputes or differences arising between the parties. If the arbitrator has numberpower to award interest pendente lite, the party claiming it would have to approach the companyrt for that purpose, even though he may have obtained satisfaction in respect of other claims from the arbitrator. This would lead to multiplicity of proceedings. An arbitrator is the creature of an agreement. Thawardas has number been followed in the later decisions of this Court. It has been explained and distinguished on the basis that in that case there was numberclaim for interest but only a claim for unliquidated damages. It has been said repeatedly that observations in the said judgment were number intended to lay down any such absolute or universal rule as they appear to on first impression. Until Jena case almost all the companyrts in the companyntry had upheld the power of the arbitrator to award interest pendente lite. Continuity and certainty is a highly desirable feature of law. Interest pendente lite is number a matter of substantive law, like interest for the period anterior to reference  pre- reference period . For doing companyplete justice between the parties, such power has always been inferred. As to post-award interest, the point is companyered by the decision of this Court in Hindustan Construction Co. Ltd. vs. State of J K , 1992  4  SCC 217. It was held there that an arbitrator is companypetent to award interest for the period from the date of the award to the date of decree or date of realization, whichever is earlier. In the case in hand, the respondents claim was in regard to two periods one from August 3, 1991 to December 31, 1992 when the agreement was subsisting and the parties were bound by its terms, and the other from January 1, 1993 to August 31, 1994 when the agreement was admittedly terminated and the respondent was carrying on the work on the request of the appellant. The Railway Administration will, however, make every endeavour for payment of the bills or other amount due to the companytractor within a reasonable time.  emphasis added  The Division Bench of the High Court took the view that Clause 31 of the agreement operated as a bar only between the parties but it would number affect the authority of the arbitrator to grant interest for the pre reference period and pendente lite. In this companynection the High Court has referred to the decisions of this Court in Executive Engineer, Dhenkanal Minor Irrigation Division, Orissa  supra , Executive Engineer  Irrigation  vs. Abhaduta Jena,  1988  1 SCC 418  which was overruled by Executive Engineer, Dhenkanal  and Secretary, Irrigation Department, Govt. of Orissa vs. G.C. Roy,  1992  1 SCC 508,  which was referred to in Executive Engineer, Dhenkanal . We are, therefore, clearly of the view that numberpre-reference or pendente lite interest was payable to the respondent on the amount under Item No.3 and the arbitrators award allowing pre-reference and pendente lite interest on that amount was plainly in breach of the express term of the agreement.
